## Navigation Menu. # 401 responses MUST have a `WWW-Authenticate` header. ## Description. express-basic-auth/README.md. |  | Per default the middleware will not add a `WWW-Authenticate` challenge header to |. You can enable that by adding `challenge: true` |. express-basic-auth/index.js. |  | res.set('WWW-Authenticate', challengeString) |. The current default behavior, responding with the status code 401 without the `WWW-Authenticate` header field, **violates RFC 9110.** Do you have any particular reasons for the decision on the default behavior that is not RFC-compliant? # RFC 9110 — HTTP semantics. The `401 (Unauthorized)` status code indicates that the request has not been applied because it lacks valid authentication credentials for the target resource. The server generating a 401 response ***MUST*** send a `WWW-Authenticate` header field (Section 11.6.1) containing at least one challenge applicable to the target resource. # Suggestion. S3.title: SEP-985: Align OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata with RFC 9728 - Model Context Protocol
S3.excerpt:
This proposal brings the MCP spec’s handling of OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata in line with RFC 9728. Currently, the MCP spec requires the use of the HTTP WWW-Authenticate header when returning a 401 Unauthorized to indicate the location of the protected resource metadata. However, RFC 9728, Section 5 states: “A protected resource MAY use the WWW-Authenticate HTTP response header field, as discussed in RFC 9110, to return a URL to its protected resource metadata to the client.” This [...] Attempt the MCP request without a token.
 If a 401 Unauthorized response is received: Check for a WWW-Authenticate header. If present and includes the resource\_metadata parameter, use it to locate the resource metadata.
 If the header is absent or does not include resource\_metadata, fallback to requesting /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource.

This change allows more flexible deployment models without removing existing capabilities.

bundles.question: In HTTP/1.1 semantics, what does the status code 401 Unauthorized mean, according to the relevant HTTP specification (e.g., RFC 9110) including any required headers/conditions such as WWW-Authenticate?
bundles.summary:
- **Meaning of `401 (Unauthorized)` (HTTP/1.1 semantics per RFC 9110):** A server-generated `401` response indicates that the **request has not been applied** because the client **lacks valid authentication credentials** for the target resource. [https://github.com/LionC/express-basic-auth/issues/51]
- **Required response header/condition:** When generating a `401` response, the server **must** include a **`WWW-Authenticate`** header field containing **at least one challenge** applicable to the target resource (RFC 9110 references this requirement in its `11.6.1` section). [https://github.com/LionC/express-basic-auth/issues/51]

(Additional context from related specs: an example protocol flow (MCP) explicitly instructs clients to check for a `WWW-Authenticate` header when receiving HTTP 401, citing RFC 9110 and RFC 9728 as the basis for the header’s role.) [https://modelcontextprotocol.io/seps/985-align-oauth-20-protected-resource-metadata-with-rf]
gaps: The provided results do not include direct, authoritative quoted text from RFC 9110 itself—only secondary quotations/assertions about it (e.g., references to “Section 11.6.1” and MUST-level requirements).
No complete list of any other `401`-related required headers/conditions from RFC 9110 is present in the retrieved results (beyond `WWW-Authenticate`).
The results do not show RFC 9110’s exact wording about the `WWW-Authenticate` challenge contents/format (e.g., whether any specific parameters are mandatory for particular authentication schemes).

No clarification is provided in the retrieved results about how `401` interacts with other HTTP semantics (e.g., whether a `WWW-Authenticate` header is required when authentication credentials are missing vs invalid, beyond the general MUST statement).

bundles.question: In HTTP/1.1 semantics, what does the status code 403 Forbidden mean, according to the relevant HTTP specification (e.g., RFC 9110)?
bundles.summary: RFC 9110 defines **403 Forbidden** as a response where the **server understood the request** but **refuses to fulfill it** (i.e., refuses to process the request for the target resource, typically due to policy/access reasons). [https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html] MDN summarizes the same semantics as: the server understood the request but refused to process it. [https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/403]
gaps: The provided sources do not include the specific RFC 9110 subsection text explicitly contrasting 403 with 401 Unauthorized; no direct RFC excerpt for that distinction is included in the search results.

bundles.question: According to the relevant HTTP specification (e.g., RFC 9110) and/or widely used authoritative guidance, when should a server return 401 Unauthorized rather than 403 Forbidden (and when should it return 403 instead of 401), including distinctions such as authentication vs authorization and whether re-authentication is possible?
bundles.summary:
- **401 Unauthorized** is used when **authentication failed or credentials were not provided** (i.e., the server doesn’t know who the client is). WorkOS summarizes: “401 Unauthorized doesn’t mean the user lacks permission. It means authentication failed or was not provided” and attributes this to RFC 9110 guidance. [https://workos.com/blog/http-error-codes]
- **401 vs 403 (authentication vs authorization):** Authgear describes 401 as meaning the server doesn’t know who the user is (credentials are missing/invalid/expired) and that the client should be able to **authenticate (again) and retry**. [https://www.authgear.com/post/http-401-vs-403]
- **When credentials are already included:** One source notes that if the request already included Authorization credentials, then a **401** indicates that **authorization has been refused for those credentials** (i.e., authentication/credential acceptance failed, not that the user is authenticated but blocked). [https://robertlathanh.com/2012/06/http-status-codes-401-unauthorized-and-403-forbidden-for-authentication-and-authorization-and-oauth]
- **403 Forbidden** is used when the resource exists but the client **is authenticated but lacks sufficient privileges** (authorization is denied). Stack Overflow gives an example: the page exists, but the user does not have sufficient privileges (e.g., not logged in or not in the proper group). [https://stackoverflow.com/questions/3297048/403-forbidden-vs-401-unauthorized-http-responses]

**Re-authentication possibility (distinction implied by guidance):**
- For **401**, guidance emphasizes that the client should be prompted to **authenticate again and retry**. [https://www.authgear.com/post/http-401-vs-403]

**Note on strict RFC quoting:** The sources generally attribute the semantics to RFC 9110, but the search results do not include direct RFC excerpt text beyond the WorkOS statement referencing RFC 9110. [https://workos.com/blog/http-error-codes]
gaps: The provided sources do not contain the exact RFC 9110 wording or specific section references explaining the precise decision rules for when to choose 401 vs 403 (e.g., any explicit conditions for use of 401 with/without `WWW-Authenticate`, and any explicit authorization-failure cases). [https://workos.com/blog/http-error-codes]

Unclear whether any source distinguishes cases where the user is authenticated but access is forbidden (authorization) vs cases where authentication is incomplete/invalid, in a way that fully maps to RFC 9110 requirements; some sources blur “not logged in” with authorization denial. [https://stackoverflow.com/questions/3297048/403-forbidden-vs-401-unauthorized-http-responses]

No provided source explicitly covers whether the server is required to include `WWW-Authenticate` (or not) when returning 401, nor how that affects client re-authentication, as described in RFC 9110. (Not present in search results.)
No provided source states explicit guidance on caching, idempotency, or retry behavior differences between 401 and 403 beyond general re-authentication implication. (Not present in search results.)
